summary: Most HTTP authentication schemes can be probed, so unauthenticated clients can learn that a server has resources needing authentication. This document defines the Concealed HTTP Authentication scheme, which hides that fact from clients that cannot authenticate.

eli5.summary: Normally a locked door tells everyone it is locked. This makes the door look like an ordinary wall to anyone without the key.

questions: how to hide that a server requires authentication
what is the concealed http authentication scheme
how does concealed authentication avoid probing
what tls versions does concealed authentication require
subtitle: An HTTP login that stays invisible: servers never issue a challenge, so unauthenticated clients learn nothing.

tldr.problem: Most HTTP authentication schemes are probeable: an origin that sends a challenge to unauthenticated clients reveals that it serves resources requiring authentication. Cryptographic signatures need a fresh nonce, and until now sharing one exposed that fact.
tldr.mechanism: The client signs data derived from a TLS keying material exporter, which is fresh for each TLS connection, and sends the signature in the Authorization header field. The server never has to send a challenge.
tldr.outcome: A server can accept authenticated clients and give everyone else the same response it gives for nonexistent resources, so the protected resources cannot be probed for.

facts.label: Minimum TLS
facts.value: TLS 1.3, or TLS 1.2 with extended master secret

today: RFC 9729 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Probing Problem
sections.content:
HTTP authentication schemes let an origin restrict some resources to authenticated requests. Usually the origin sends a challenge and the client answers it. That makes the origin probeable: anyone can ask, receive a challenge, and learn that something is being protected.

Sometimes an origin wants to offer a service only to "those who know", and give everyone else no sign that it exists. The RFC gives two examples: a company offering employee access to services on its own website, and members of a community using ephemeral keys to reach geography- or capability-specific resources. Both rely on keys being distributed by some external mechanism.

Signature-based schemes such as HOBA (RFC 7486) exist, but the origin must send a fresh challenge so the signature input is fresh. That challenge is exactly what gives the origin away.
sections.eli5: Imagine a secret clubhouse that answers every knock with a loud "members only!" Everyone now knows there is a club. This RFC is about a clubhouse that stays silent unless you know the secret.

sections.title: How the Concealed Scheme Works
sections.content:
The Concealed scheme uses asymmetric cryptography. Clients hold a key ID and a public/private key pair, and the origin keeps a mapping from authorized key IDs to public keys.

Instead of waiting for a nonce from the server, the client uses a TLS keying material exporter to generate data to sign. Both ends of a TLS connection can compute the same exporter output, so the freshness comes from the connection itself and nothing extra has to cross the wire. The client sends the signature in the Authorization (or Proxy-Authorization) header field, with extra details carried as authentication parameters. The server checks the signature against its database of known keys and uses the result, for example, to restrict access.
sections.eli5: You and the doorman both know a secret phrase that changes with every visit, because it comes from the private handshake you just shared. You prove you know it by signing it, without the doorman ever having to ask.

sections.title: What the Client Computes
sections.content:
A client SHALL compute its proof with a TLS keying material exporter using the label EXPORTER-HTTP-Concealed-Authentication, a context structure described below, and an output length of 48 bytes. TLS 1.3 exporters come from RFC 8446; TLS 1.2 exporters come from RFC 5705.

The context is built from the signature algorithm, the key ID, the public key, and the scheme, host, port and realm of the request. Lengths use the variable-length integer encoding from RFC 9000 and MUST use the minimum number of bytes. The signature algorithm and port are 16-bit integers in network byte order. If no realm is configured, the realm is empty and the client MUST NOT send the realm parameter.

Of the 48 output bytes, the first 32 are the Signature Input and the next 16 are the Verification value, sent alongside the signature so the recipient can confirm that its exporter produced the right values.

The signature covers the concatenation of the octet 32 repeated 64 times, the string HTTP Concealed Authentication, a single 0 byte as separator, and the Signature Input. This static prefix mirrors the TLS 1.3 CertificateVerify construction and limits damage if a key is accidentally reused across protocols.
sections.eli5: The client mixes the shared secret from the handshake with a fixed label and the website it is visiting, then stamps it with its personal seal. The fixed label stops the seal from being reused in some other game.

sections.title: Authentication Parameters
sections.content:
Five parameters travel in the header field, and all five are REQUIRED. Byte sequences are base64url without quotes and without padding, so they contain only ASCII letters, digits, dash and underscore. The one integer parameter has no minus sign and no leading zeroes.

The a parameter repeats the public key so the server can compare it with its own copy, which avoids key confusion issues. The v parameter avoids issues with signature schemes where some keys can produce signatures valid for several inputs. The s value is an integer from 0 to 65535 taken from the IANA TLS SignatureScheme registry.

Public keys are encoded according to the algorithm: RSASSA-PSS uses a DER-encoded RSAPublicKey (non-DER BER MUST be rejected), ECDSA uses the uncompressed point representation from the TLS specification, and EdDSA uses its own byte string encoding. Other algorithms need a separate document defining their encoding.
sections.eli5: The client hands over five small notes: who I am, my public stamp, my proof, which kind of stamp I used, and a quick check number. The server needs all five or it ignores the whole thing.

sections.title: Frontends, Backends and Server Checks
sections.content:
The RFC splits the server into a frontend, which terminates the TLS or QUIC connection, and a backend, which holds the database of key IDs and public keys. Usually both live in one origin server, but the frontend can be a gateway in front of a separate origin.

The frontend parses the header field and MUST ignore the whole field if any parameter is missing or unparseable. When the roles are split, the frontend forwards the original header plus a new Concealed-Auth-Export request header field containing the 48-byte exporter output as a Structured Field Byte Sequence. Backends MUST ignore that field unless they trust the sender, and frontends MUST NOT forward one received from a client.

The backend checks that the parameters parse, that the key ID is in its database, that the stored public key equals the one in the header, that the verification value matches the exporter output, and that the signature verifies. If any check fails, it MUST treat the request as if the Authorization header were missing.
sections.eli5: One helper at the front gate hears the secret handshake, and another helper in the back room keeps the guest list. If the front gate and back room are different people, the gate tells the back room what it heard, and the back room only believes people it trusts.

sections.title: Staying Non-Probeable and TLS Requirements
sections.content:
A server that wants unprobeable resources MUST answer authentication failures with exactly the response it gives for nonexistent resources, for example status 404 instead of 401. Checking signatures takes time, so an attacker might compare response timing; servers can slightly delay responses for some nonexistent resources, taking care that the delay itself does not give the mechanism away. Hidden resources also must not be linked from any unauthenticated page or discoverable out of band.

The scheme is defined only for HTTP over TLS, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Because exporters are only safe for authentication when bound to the TLS session, it requires either TLS 1.3 or later, or TLS 1.2 with the extended master secret extension (RFC 7627). Clients MUST NOT use it otherwise, and servers MUST treat such requests as if authentication were absent.
sections.eli5: If the club wants to stay secret, a stranger who knocks must get the same blank wall as at any empty house, and it must take about the same time to answer. There must also be no signposts pointing to the door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The scheme guarantees freshness without the server sending a nonce, so the server need not reveal that it expects authentication. Clients also avoid leaking the presence of authentication through cleartext TLS Client Hello extensions.

Freshness can be as old as the TLS connection, and servers wanting better freshness can force new connections, for example with the HTTP/3 GOAWAY frame. Proofs are not bound to individual requests, so on one connection they are identical. Clients that multiplex different security contexts over one connection must ensure those contexts cannot read each other's header fields, or one could replay another's Authorization header. The RFC says modern web browsers meet this constraint.

Keys used with this scheme MUST NOT be reused in other protocols. Origins can link requests that use the same key, but requests are not linkable across origins if the keys are specific to each origin.
sections.eli5: The proof is fresh for each private connection, but within one connection it stays the same, like a wristband good for the whole visit. So the visitor must not let anyone else on the same bus read the wristband.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered three things. The authentication scheme name Concealed is in the HTTP Authentication Schemes registry. The exporter label EXPORTER-HTTP-Concealed-Authentication is in the TLS Exporter Labels registry, marked as not OK for DTLS and as recommended. The header field Concealed-Auth-Export is in the HTTP Field Name Registry as permanent with the structured type Item.
sections.eli5: The three new names were written in the official list of names, so nobody else picks the same ones by accident.

items.label: Key ID
items.desc: Byte sequence naming which key the client is using; the backend uses it to find the key in its database.

items.label: Public key
items.desc: Byte sequence holding the public key the server uses to verify the signature.

items.label: Signature scheme
items.desc: Integer from 0 to 65535 from the IANA TLS SignatureScheme registry.

items.label: Verification
items.desc: Byte sequence holding the 16 bytes of exporter output after the 32-byte signature input.

viz.caption: THE 48-BYTE EXPORTER OUTPUT AND WHAT IS SIGNED

items.title: Signature Input
items.text: First 32 bytes of exporter output; signed after the static prefix.

items.title: Verification
items.text: Next 16 bytes; sent in the v parameter so the server can confirm its exporter matches.

items.title: Static prefix
items.text: Octet 32 repeated 64 times, the string HTTP Concealed Authentication, then one 0 byte.
